h1: 7 Compact Leaf Blowers for Small Yards and Patios, Ranked & Reviewed (2026)
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 compact leaf blowers for small yards, patios and decks, compared on airflow, power source, battery kits and price.
summary: The Makita DUB185Z is the compact blower to buy if you want a quality 18V LXT tool you can keep using for years. The BLACK+DECKER is the cheap, simple electric pick for patios, the WOLFMEN gives you a 450 CFM headline for under $100, and the MZK is the lowest-cost way to get a cordless blower at all.
intro: Small yards trip people up in a specific way: they assume a small job needs a weak tool, and then buy the lightest, flimsiest blower on the shelf. A tiny blower with a tiny battery runs out of puff halfway down a driveway, and you finish with a broom anyway. The right size is the smallest tool that still has enough air behind it to clear what your yard actually drops.

We ranked seven compact blowers from their spec sheets and listings, looking at listed airflow, how they are powered, whether batteries come in the box and the price bucket. Some listings publish no airflow figure at all, and where that is true we mark it as a gap instead of guessing.

products.name: Makita DUB185Z Cordless Handheld Leaf Blower Powered by 18V LXT
products.verdict: A proper 18V LXT handheld that borrows batteries from the rest of a Makita kit.
products.description:
The DUB185Z is a cordless handheld that runs on Makita's 18V LXT battery family and ships as a bare tool in the $50 to $100 bracket. The listing does not publish an airflow figure, so judge it on the platform it belongs to rather than a headline number.

It ranks first because the LXT range is among the most widely stocked cordless systems in the world, so batteries, chargers and service are never hard to find. Most of the cheaper blowers in this ranking are sealed into their own battery, which makes them disposable when the pack fades. The tradeoff is that you buy the battery and charger separately if you do not already own them, which raises the real entry price.

Buy it if you own any LXT tools or plan to. Skip it if you want a self-contained kit for a single weekend job.
pros: Strong brand service and parts support
cons: No airflow figure on the listing
products.idealFor: Makita owners who want a small blower that shares existing batteries.
products.skipIf: You need everything in one box for one low price.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A no-fuss, low-cost electric blower from a brand that is easy to get serviced.
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER lists 180 CFM in a handheld body at $25 to $50. The listing calls it an electric blower and does not say cordless, and that class of tool usually draws power from a wall outlet, so plan for an extension cord and a reach limit.

It ranks second because a mains-powered blower never fades the way a small battery does, and 180 CFM is plenty for a deck, a stoop or a short driveway. It sits behind the Makita because you are tied to the cord and the airflow is modest, but it costs half as much and has nothing to charge.

It is the right pick for a townhouse or a tight lot near an outlet. Skip it if your leaves are far from the house or you dislike dragging a cord around shrubs.
pros: No battery to charge or replace
Trusted brand with easy parts access
cons: Modest airflow for heavy leaf fall
products.idealFor: Small lots and patios within reach of an outdoor outlet.
products.skipIf: You want to roam the whole yard cord-free.

products.name: WOLFMEN Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A cordless 450 CFM listing in the $50 to $100 bracket, with the usual unbranded caveats.
products.description:
The WOLFMEN is a cordless blower that lists 450 CFM, a much higher volume number than the 180 CFM class. That is a quoted peak figure, and unbranded makers rarely say how it was measured, so treat it as a sign of intent rather than a guarantee.

It ranks third because the airflow headline is the biggest in this group at a mid-range price, and it frees you from a cord. It sits below the BLACK+DECKER only because that pick has a recognized service network, whereas replacement batteries for generic units depend on the seller staying in business.

It works for a small lawn with light leaf fall where you want cordless freedom and some power in reserve. Skip it if you expect a ten-year tool.
pros: Cordless with no cord to drag
products.idealFor: Small-lawn owners who want cordless airflow on a modest budget.
products.skipIf: You want brand-backed service for years.

products.name: MZK 20V Cordless Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A 450 CFM cordless listing at the lowest price bracket in this group.
products.description:
The MZK is a 20V cordless handheld that lists 450 CFM and falls in the $25 to $50 bracket. It is the least expensive way into cordless blowing here, which makes it easy to justify as a second tool.

It ranks fourth, behind the WOLFMEN, because the two share the same airflow headline and the WOLFMEN costs only a little more while giving buyers more of a premium feel in its bracket. The MZK beats the next picks on listed airflow, since JAGROM publishes 180 CFM and the others publish none.

It is a sensible buy for a balcony, a short driveway or a garage floor. Skip it if you want long runtimes, since a pack at this price rarely supports a full-yard job.
pros: Lowest price for a cordless blower
Easy to store in a closet
Low risk as a backup tool
cons: Runtime is limited on one pack
products.idealFor: Balcony and townhouse owners who need a cheap cordless tool.
products.skipIf: You will clear a full yard in a single session.

products.name: JAGROM Leaf Blower Cordless with 2 Battery and Charger
products.verdict: Two batteries and a charger make the 180 CFM output go further.
products.description:
The JAGROM combines a 180 CFM cordless handheld with two batteries and a charger, all in the $25 to $50 bracket. With two packs you can run one while the other charges, which is a smart answer to the main weakness of small cordless tools.

It lands fifth because 180 CFM is well below the 450 CFM headline picks, so it works slower on anything but dry, light debris. The kit value is the reason it still ranks above the listings that publish no airflow. It matches the BLACK+DECKER on airflow but gives up the unlimited runtime of a mains-powered tool.

Choose it for decks, porches and gravel paths. Skip it if damp or heavy leaf piles are a regular chore.
pros: Two batteries come in the box
Swap packs to extend work time
Low entry price for a kit
cons: Airflow is on the low side
Unbranded packs may be hard to replace
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a complete cordless kit for hard surfaces.
products.skipIf: You expect it to move wet leaves.

products.name: YOOVL Leaf Blower Cordless
products.verdict: A cordless handheld in the $50 to $100 bracket with no airflow number to check.
products.description:
The YOOVL is a cordless handheld blower priced at $50 to $100, with no CFM figure given on its page, so there is no clean way to compare it with the WOLFMEN or the JAGROM at similar prices.

It ranks sixth because buying at this price without a published output is a gamble when other picks give you numbers. It earns a spot over the FAOGO because it is a simpler, single-pack proposition, though that is a judgment of positioning, not a measured difference.

It can serve a small patio owner who prefers this format and brand mix. Skip it if you like to compare airflow on paper before you spend.
products.idealFor: Patio owners who are happy to buy without a CFM number.
products.skipIf: You want spec-based confidence before buying.

products.name: FAOGO Cordless Leaf Blower with 2 Batteries & Charger - 990,000 RPM
products.verdict: A two-battery kit whose headline RPM figure tells you little about real output.
products.description:
The FAOGO is a cordless handheld that includes two batteries and a charger. Its listing leads with a very large RPM number, but motor speed alone says almost nothing about nozzle airflow, and no CFM figure is given.

It ranks last because the missing airflow data weakens the case against the YOOVL and the kit-based JAGROM, which both give buyers something firmer to judge. The second battery is the saving grace, since spares are the first accessory owners add.

It makes sense if you want two packs in a single box. Skip it if you want to compare airflow before purchase.
pros: Two batteries included in the kit
cons: RPM headline is not real output
products.idealFor: Buyers who prioritize a bundled spare battery.
products.skipIf: You want a verified airflow figure.

whatMatters.detail: A corded electric blower never runs flat but needs an outlet and a cord. A cordless one roams freely but is limited by its pack. Decide first which constraint suits your yard, then read the listing for the words electric, cordless or battery included.

CFM is cubic feet of air moved per minute, and it is the best single number for how fast a blower clears dry debris. Around 180 CFM suits a deck, while 450 CFM handles a small lawn. If a listing gives no figure, assume you are buying blind.

A battery that fits other tools, like Makita's 18V LXT, keeps the blower useful after a sealed pack wears out. Sealed packs on generic kits are fine for light seasonal use. Check whether the listing says bare tool, which means no battery or charger.

You hold a handheld blower out at arm's length, so small differences in weight feel large after five minutes. Lighter tools reduce fatigue but usually carry smaller packs. Look for the listed weight and prefer a body where the battery sits behind the nozzle.

Electric blowers are far quieter than gas models, but some towns still restrict hours or decibel levels. A listed noise rating helps if you live close to your neighbors. When none is given, plan to use the blower mid-morning rather than early.

cards.text: The BLACK+DECKER Electric is the simplest option for a deck, and the JAGROM kit suits porches where you can swap packs mid-task.

cards.text: You own other Makita tools or want a blower that will last many seasons. The Makita DUB185Z earns its extra cost through the LXT battery ecosystem.

cards.text: You only clear a patio a few times a year. The MZK or the BLACK+DECKER Electric does the work for under $50.

faq.q: Will Makita LXT batteries fit the DUB185Z?
faq.a: Yes, the DUB185Z is built around the 18V LXT platform, so any LXT battery and compatible charger will run it. The tool ships bare, so buy a pack separately if you do not own one.

faq.q: What is the common mistake with small leaf blowers?
faq.a: Choosing the smallest, lightest body without checking the battery or cord. A tool that cannot sustain airflow for ten minutes turns every job into a stop-start chore.

faq.q: Is the Makita worth it over a cheap cordless kit?
faq.a: Yes if you have other 18V tools or want years of battery availability. If you only need a seasonal patio tool, the MZK or JAGROM does the job at far lower cost.

faq.q: How do I set up a cordless blower for the first time?
faq.a: Charge the pack fully, fit the nozzle until it clicks and run the blower on its lowest speed first. Move up to higher settings only for stuck or heavy debris.

faq.q: How do I maintain a compact leaf blower?
faq.a: Clear leaf dust from the air intake after each use and keep batteries somewhere dry and cool. Do not store packs fully drained for months.

faq.q: Can a small blower handle wet leaves?
faq.a: Not well. Low-airflow tools such as the BLACK+DECKER and the JAGROM are meant for dry debris, and even the 450 CFM listings need a few passes to shift damp piles.

finalTake: The Makita DUB185Z is the compact blower to own if you care about long-term battery support. The BLACK+DECKER Electric is the pick for a tight lot with an outlet nearby, and the WOLFMEN gives a big airflow headline for modest money. If you want the lowest price of entry into cordless, buy the MZK and keep the rest of your budget.
